cards.name: library
cards.summary: Texture-fill sample library file (library.txr, a UTF-16 text file in <CorelDRAW 2024 install folder>/Custom Data), read for facts: it lists 6 texture libraries holding 36, 43, 25, 33, 27 and 31 textures, 195 entries in all (193 distinct ids, because two ids sit in two libraries). Each texture is stored as a style name plus a few numbers (a random seed first, then sliders and colours): 62 distinct style names occur, among them Surfaces, Sky 5 Colors, Water 2 Colors, Mineral.Cloudy, Cosmic Energy and Satellite Photography, and 105 of the 195 use older 'Cdr5:' styles (for example Cdr5:Surfaces-Rainbow, Cdr5:Putty 3C and Cdr5:Leather 5C). The library and texture names in the file are resource ids that only the app resolves. The thumbnail is a script render: the first six textures of the first library applied to six squares, which shows a pale yellow maze-like pattern, a sky blue with white clouds, a saturated blue cloud, a rainbow radial glow in magenta, yellow and green, a salmon-pink marble and a dark green terrain pattern.
use_for: quick sample backgrounds for artwork: sky, clouds, water, marble and rock looks
organic fills that change with a seed number without placing an image
finding a starting texture to refine in the Texture fill dialog
avoid: Photographic realism: the textures are generated patterns, mostly soft and cloudy; use a photo for a real material.
Print at a large size: a texture fill is rendered at a set resolution, so check it for blockiness at poster size.
Looking the textures up by name: the names in the file are resource ids, so they cannot be listed or chosen by script from this file.
cards.applies_to: a closed vector shape's fill (the batch requires 'vector object (fill)'): the file is the library the Texture fill dialog reads, not an object you apply
cards.how_to_apply: Select a closed shape, open the Interactive Fill tool or Object Properties > Fill, choose Texture fill, pick a library and a texture in the dialog. Script: Shape.Fill.ApplyTextureFill(TextureName, LibraryName) (type-library signature; the names are resolved by the app and no COM member lists them, so scripts must use names already known from the dialog). File: <CorelDRAW 2024 install folder>/Custom Data/library.txr (text, read).

verified.note: Script render matches: pale yellow maze, sky blue with clouds, saturated blue cloud, rainbow radial glow, salmon marble, dark green terrain; the UTF-16 file parses to 6 libraries of 36/43/25/33/27/31 = 195 entries, 193 distinct ids, 62 distinct styles, 105 Cdr5, but its Cdr5 Putty and Leather styles carry 3C/5C suffixes.

review.changes: summary: example style names corrected to the file's exact names (Cdr5:Putty 3C, Cdr5:Leather 5C; there is no plain Cdr5:Putty or Cdr5:Leather)

cards.name: texture
cards.summary: Texture-fill styles file (texture.txr, a UTF-16 text file in <CorelDRAW 2024 install folder>/Custom Data), read for facts: its header lists 7 texture library ids and names one of them (CorelDefaultID_10000) as the styles library, which holds exactly 108 style definitions. Each has a plain English name and a parameter list of 3 to 12 entries (number sliders with their ranges and defaults, and RGB colours): the first 43 are base styles such as Aerial Photography, Blend Corners, Blend Edges, Cosmic Clouds, Cosmic Energy, Drapes, Fiber, Flames, Noise, Recycled Paper, Satellite Photography, Scribbles, Sky, Surfaces, Swirls, Threads, Water and Water Color; the other 65 are older 'Cdr5:' styles such as Biology, BubbleMania, Cotton, Leather, Mandel0, Pottery Wheel, Putty, Rain Drops, Rings, Ripples, Rock, Spots and Vapor, many in 2-, 3- and 5-colour versions. The thumbnail is a script render and shows six identical squares of a purple, pink and blue rough embossed texture, which suggests the render fell back to one default texture rather than drawing six different styles, so it says little about what the 108 styles look like.
use_for: knowing which texture styles exist (clouds, minerals, water, noise, leather, putty and more) before choosing one in the dialog
planning a texture fill: each style's ranges show what can be varied
choosing between 2-, 3- and 5-colour versions of a style
avoid: Trusting the thumbnail: the six squares are the same texture, so they do not show the styles.
Applying it as a fill: the file is a catalogue of styles, not a texture you can pick; choose a texture in the Texture fill dialog.
Looking the styles up by script: the library and texture names are resource ids that only the app resolves.
cards.applies_to: a closed vector shape's fill (the batch requires 'vector object (fill)'): the file is the library the Texture fill dialog reads, not an object you apply
cards.how_to_apply: Select a closed shape, open the Interactive Fill tool or Object Properties > Fill, choose Texture fill and pick a texture in the dialog (the dialog's style parameters come from this catalogue). Script: Shape.Fill.ApplyTextureFill(TextureName, LibraryName) (type-library signature; names resolved by the app). File: <CorelDRAW 2024 install folder>/Custom Data/texture.txr (text, read).

verified.note: Script render matches: six identical purple-pink-blue embossed squares, as the card warns; the file parses to 7 header library ids, styles library CorelDefaultID_10000 with 108 styles (43 base, 65 Cdr5) of 3 to 12 parameters each.

cards.name: BARK
cards.summary: Texture bitmap (a TIFF in <CorelDRAW 2024 install folder>/Custom Data/Textures). The thumbnail is the file's own image drawn from the file (the files are only 128 x 128 px, so most thumbnails are enlarged). It shows a tall, vertically ridged tree-bark surface in blue-grey and dark brown, with deep dark crevices between the ridges. File: 128 x 128 px TIFF, 8-bit palette (256 colours), 72 ppi, 18,338 bytes. Tiling check: the difference between opposite edges is 1.11 times (across) and 1.15 times (down) the ordinary neighbouring-pixel difference, so it should repeat without a visible seam.
avoid: Smooth, modern looks: the surface is rough and dark.
Large areas at high resolution: the picture is only 128 x 128 px, so enlarging it to poster size shows soft, blocky pixels.
